title: Own Your Exit
promise: Why cheap leaving keeps a place fair, and how to own what you'd take with you.

cards.text: A restaurant can keep a dress code because you can walk across the street. *House rules stay fair when leaving is cheap.*
On most apps your name, your followers and your posts live inside the app. Leaving means starting from zero, so its house rules start to work like laws.
So own the parts yourself: your name, your connections, your work. Then the app is one front door among many, and you can use another or build your own.
*Your name.* An account number in a public registry, owned by a key you hold, not by any app. Guard that key like the deed to a house.
*Your keys.* Give each app its own narrow key, never the deed. A valet key starts the car but won't open the trunk, and you can take it back.
*Your connections and work.* Each follow and post is signed by you, so any app can show it and anyone can check it. You rent the storage yearly.

cards.def: Not a right on paper but a path you can actually walk: you can leave a group and take your name, your connections and your work with you.

cards.heading: Three commands and a witness
cards.text: In October 2026, about two dozen guides appeared for running a social network yourself: your own node holding the full network, your own app reading from it, no company's permission needed. The convincing ones came with a witness: a stranger who followed every step and said publicly that it worked. One builder synced the whole network, logged every command, and proposed ten changes to the original project.

cards.claim: Exit is cheap for developers, not for most people. Running your own node means a server with 2 TB of disk and comfort at a terminal. And leaving with your follower list is not the same as your friends coming with you.
cards.reply: Largely true. But to keep the default app in check, most people don't need to leave. Leaving needs to be possible and visible, and every guide a stranger can finish makes it cheaper. Whether ordinary people will ever switch in numbers is an open question.

cards.text: If the app you use most changed its rules tomorrow, what could you take with you, and what would you leave behind?

cards.prompt: Own one piece of your digital life this week: your name, your connections or your work. Start with the one you'd miss most.
steps: Export it into a folder you control, then open the file to check it's all there.
Find a login only one company can recover, and add a backup way in that you control.
Trying a run-it-yourself guide? Use a test account first, never your main one.
Never paste a recovery phrase into a script or a website.
